title: CTS Psalms — Unit 10: Psalm 55, Casting Your Burden

blocks.en: 📖 The Book of Psalms — Unit 10: Psalm 55, Casting Your Burden
blocks.es_reference: 📖 El Libro de los Salmos — Unidad 10: Salmo 55, Echando Tu Carga

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "Cast your burden on the Lord, and He shall sustain you; He shall never permit the righteous to be moved." — Psalm 55:22 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Echa sobre Jehová tu carga, y él te sustentará; no dejará para siempre caído al justo." — Salmo 55:22 (RVG)

blocks.en: 1. The Abrasive Edge of a Fallen World
blocks.es_reference: 1. El Borde Áspero de un Mundo Caído

blocks.en: Life is not all sunshine and ease. There are tough seasons when nothing flows as neatly as a seminar notebook would suggest, when the heavens seem to be brass and our prayers seem to fall back unanswered. Even the prophet Jeremiah cried out under the sheer weight of the bad news he was given to deliver. There is an abrasive edge to reality in a fallen world, and pretending otherwise helps no one. Part of the work of faith — and part of the work of every pastor — is learning to face that edge honestly, and to help others face it, rather than papering it over with easy words.
blocks.es_reference: La vida no es todo sol y comodidad. Hay temporadas difíciles en que nada fluye tan ordenadamente como sugeriría el cuaderno de un seminario, cuando el cielo parece de bronce y nuestras oraciones parecen caer sin respuesta. Aun el profeta Jeremías clamó bajo el puro peso de las malas noticias que le tocaba anunciar. Hay un borde áspero en la realidad de un mundo caído, y fingir lo contrario no ayuda a nadie. Parte de la obra de la fe — y parte de la obra de todo pastor — es aprender a enfrentar ese borde con honestidad, y ayudar a otros a enfrentarlo, en lugar de disimularlo con palabras fáciles.

blocks.en: Psalm 55 is written from inside that hard place. David is overwhelmed; his heart is "severely pained within" him, and he longs for wings like a dove to fly away and be at rest. He does not pretend the burden is light. But at the center of the psalm he arrives at a single, steadying command, and it is the verse this lesson is built upon: "Cast your burden on the LORD, and He shall sustain you." The whole question of the Christian life under pressure is gathered into that one sentence. What do we do with a weight we did not choose and cannot lift? We give it to God.
blocks.es_reference: El Salmo 55 está escrito desde dentro de ese lugar difícil. David está abrumado; su corazón está "dolorido dentro" de él, y anhela alas como de paloma para volar lejos y hallar descanso. No finge que la carga sea liviana. Pero en el centro del salmo llega a un solo mandato firme, y es el versículo sobre el cual se construye esta lección: "Echa sobre Jehová tu carga, y él te sustentará." Toda la cuestión de la vida cristiana bajo presión se reúne en esa sola frase. ¿Qué hacemos con un peso que no escogimos y no podemos levantar? Se lo damos a Dios.

blocks.en: 2. What It Means to Cast
blocks.es_reference: 2. Qué Significa Echar

blocks.en: Psalm 55:22 (NKJV): "Cast your burden on the LORD, and He shall sustain you; He shall never permit the righteous to be moved."
blocks.es_reference: Salmo 55:22 (RVG): "Echa sobre Jehová tu carga, y él te sustentará; no dejará para siempre caído al justo."

blocks.en: The word translated "cast" is forceful. It is not a gentle setting-down but a deliberate throwing — the same idea as flinging a heavy load off your own shoulders and onto someone else's. That matters, because a burden is not cast by merely worrying about it more religiously. To cast a burden is a decisive act of the will: we consciously transfer the weight from ourselves, who cannot bear it, to God, who can. Peter would later echo this very verse: "casting all your care upon Him, for He cares for you" (1 Peter 5:7).
blocks.es_reference: La palabra traducida "echa" es enérgica. No es un suave depositar, sino un arrojar deliberado — la misma idea de lanzar una carga pesada de los propios hombros a los de otro. Eso importa, porque una carga no se echa simplemente preocupándose por ella de manera más religiosa. Echar una carga es un acto decisivo de la voluntad: trasladamos conscientemente el peso de nosotros mismos, que no podemos llevarlo, a Dios, que sí puede. Pedro haría eco de este mismo versículo: "echando toda vuestra ansiedad sobre él, porque él tiene cuidado de vosotros" (1 Pedro 5:7).

blocks.en: Notice carefully what God promises in return. He does not promise to remove the burden; He promises to "sustain you." The Hebrew pictures God as the one who holds you up, who bears you so that you can bear the load. The second line says it again from the other side: "He shall never permit the righteous to be moved" — not that the righteous will never feel the weight, but that they will never be toppled by it. The believer under pressure is like a tree in a storm whose roots hold; the wind is real, the bending is real, but the falling never comes.
blocks.es_reference: Note con cuidado lo que Dios promete a cambio. No promete quitar la carga; promete "sustentarte." El hebreo presenta a Dios como el que te sostiene, el que te lleva para que tú puedas llevar el peso. La segunda línea lo dice de nuevo desde el otro lado: "no dejará para siempre caído al justo" — no que el justo nunca sienta el peso, sino que nunca será derribado por él. El creyente bajo presión es como un árbol en la tormenta cuyas raíces resisten; el viento es real, la inclinación es real, pero la caída nunca llega.

blocks.en: 3. When Life Tumbles In
blocks.es_reference: 3. Cuando la Vida se Derrumba

blocks.en: This is a truth that can only be tested where it costs something, and church history offers few clearer tests than Arthur John Gossip. He was a respected Scottish preacher whose wife died suddenly in her middle years, leaving him desolate. Friends told him not to try to preach so soon, but on the very next Sunday he climbed the pulpit stairs and preached a sermon some have called one of the greatest of the twentieth century: "But When Life Tumbles In, What Then?"
blocks.es_reference: Esta es una verdad que solo puede probarse donde cuesta algo, y la historia de la iglesia ofrece pocas pruebas más claras que la de Arthur John Gossip. Era un respetado predicador escocés cuya esposa murió de repente en la mediana edad, dejándolo desolado. Los amigos le dijeron que no intentara predicar tan pronto, pero el domingo siguiente subió las escaleras del púlpito y predicó un sermón que algunos han llamado uno de los más grandes del siglo veinte: "Pero Cuando la Vida se Derrumba, ¿Qué Entonces?"

blocks.en: "Where Else Is There to Turn?": Gossip told his grieving congregation, "You people in the sunshine may believe the faith, but we in the shadow must believe it. We have nothing else." He admitted that some, in such sorrow, are tempted to turn away from God altogether — and then he asked the question that has no other answer: "Where else is there to turn?" He closed by imagining himself stepping into the cold, rushing river of death, and calling back to those who must one day cross it themselves, in the words of Hopeful in Pilgrim's Progress: "Be of good cheer, my brother, for I feel the bottom, and it is sound."
blocks.es_reference: "¿A Dónde Más Hay que Ir?": Gossip dijo a su congregación afligida: "Ustedes los que están en la luz del sol pueden creer la fe, pero nosotros en la sombra debemos creerla. No tenemos nada más." Admitió que algunos, en tal dolor, son tentados a apartarse de Dios por completo — y luego hizo la pregunta que no tiene otra respuesta: "¿A dónde más hay que ir?" Cerró imaginándose entrar en el río frío e impetuoso de la muerte, y llamando a los que un día deberán cruzarlo, con las palabras de Esperanzado en El Progreso del Peregrino: "Ten ánimo, hermano mío, porque siento el fondo, y es firme."

blocks.en: That is the testimony of a man who actually cast his burden and found the promise true. The faith that feels optional in the sunshine becomes the only ground left to stand on in the shadow — and it holds. As the old Scottish saint Samuel Rutherford said, "Grace grows best in the winter."
blocks.es_reference: Ese es el testimonio de un hombre que de veras echó su carga y halló cierta la promesa. La fe que parece opcional bajo el sol llega a ser el único terreno que queda para estar de pie en la sombra — y sostiene. Como dijo el viejo santo escocés Samuel Rutherford: "La gracia crece mejor en el invierno."

blocks.en: 4. The Lord of Gethsemane Bears Burdens Too
blocks.es_reference: 4. El Señor de Getsemaní También Lleva Cargas

blocks.en: We are not asked to cast our burdens on a God who has never felt the weight of one. In the Garden of Gethsemane, Jesus prayed that the cup might pass from Him. He did not want the cross; the dread of it pressed sweat like blood from His brow. And yet the cup was not taken away, because bearing it was the very reason He had come into the world. Here is the part we must not miss: though the Father did not remove the burden, neither did He abandon His Son in it. He sent an angel to strengthen Him, and gave Him the settled peace to rise from His knees and finish what He was sent to do.
blocks.es_reference: No se nos pide echar nuestras cargas sobre un Dios que jamás ha sentido el peso de una. En el huerto de Getsemaní, Jesús oró que pasara de Él la copa. No quería la cruz; el pavor de ella le hizo sudar como gotas de sangre. Y sin embargo la copa no fue quitada, porque llevarla era la razón misma por la que había venido al mundo. Aquí está lo que no debemos pasar por alto: aunque el Padre no quitó la carga, tampoco abandonó a Su Hijo en ella. Envió un ángel para fortalecerle, y le dio la paz firme para levantarse de Sus rodillas y terminar aquello para lo cual fue enviado.

blocks.en: This reshapes what we expect when we cast our burden on the Lord. We often assume that casting a burden means the burden disappears. Sometimes God in mercy does lift it. But far more often He does for us what He did for His own Son: He leaves the weight on our shoulders and puts His strength underneath it. The sustaining is the answer to the prayer. With this in view, Psalm 55 invites three deliberate acts: giving God our thanks, giving Him our grief, and giving Him the burden itself.
blocks.es_reference: Esto reconfigura lo que esperamos cuando echamos nuestra carga sobre el Señor. Solemos suponer que echar una carga significa que la carga desaparece. A veces Dios en Su misericordia sí la levanta. Pero mucho más a menudo hace por nosotros lo que hizo por Su propio Hijo: deja el peso sobre nuestros hombros y pone Su fuerza debajo de él. El sustento es la respuesta a la oración. Con esto a la vista, el Salmo 55 invita a tres actos deliberados: dar a Dios nuestra gratitud, darle nuestro dolor, y darle la carga misma.

blocks.en: 5. Give God Your Thanks
blocks.es_reference: 5. Dé a Dios Su Gratitud

blocks.en: 1 Thessalonians 5:18 (NKJV): "In everything give thanks; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you."
blocks.es_reference: 1 Tesalonicenses 5:18 (RVG): "Dad gracias en todo; porque esta es la voluntad de Dios para con vosotros en Cristo Jesús."

blocks.en: The first response is the hardest, which is precisely why it must be commanded rather than left to feeling. Read the verse carefully: it does not say give thanks for everything, as though we should be glad a tragedy struck. It says give thanks in everything — that even in the middle of the burden there remains something for which God may be thanked. Thanksgiving here is not a denial of pain; it is a deliberate turning of the eyes away from the weight and toward the One who is still good, still present, still sovereign over the very trial we are walking through.
blocks.es_reference: La primera respuesta es la más difícil, y por eso mismo debe ser mandada y no dejada al sentimiento. Lea el versículo con cuidado: no dice dad gracias por todo, como si debiéramos alegrarnos de que ocurriera una tragedia. Dice dad gracias en todo — que aun en medio de la carga queda algo por lo cual se puede dar gracias a Dios. La gratitud aquí no es una negación del dolor; es un deliberado volver los ojos del peso hacia Aquel que sigue siendo bueno, sigue presente, sigue soberano sobre la prueba misma que atravesamos.

blocks.en: This is why thanksgiving steadies a sinking heart. Self-pity and bitterness both work by narrowing our vision until the burden fills the whole horizon and God disappears behind it. Thanksgiving pries that vision back open. It does not pretend the burden is small; it insists that the God who has given so many good gifts has not stopped being good now. Offered honestly — and never glibly to someone in fresh grief — gratitude becomes a kind of medicine, loosening the grip of despair and reminding us that this burden, heavy as it is, is not the whole of our story.
blocks.es_reference: Por eso la gratitud sostiene a un corazón que se hunde. La autocompasión y la amargura obran estrechando nuestra visión hasta que la carga llena todo el horizonte y Dios desaparece detrás de ella. La gratitud vuelve a abrir esa visión. No finge que la carga sea pequeña; insiste en que el Dios que ha dado tantos buenos regalos no ha dejado de ser bueno ahora. Ofrecida con honestidad — y nunca a la ligera a alguien en duelo reciente — la gratitud llega a ser una especie de medicina, que afloja el dominio de la desesperación y nos recuerda que esta carga, por pesada que sea, no es toda nuestra historia.

blocks.en: 6. Give God Your Grief
blocks.es_reference: 6. Dé a Dios Su Dolor

blocks.en: Matthew 5:4 (NKJV): "Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted."
blocks.es_reference: Mateo 5:4 (RVG): "Bienaventurados los que lloran, porque ellos recibirán consolación."

blocks.en: The second response is to give God our grief — not to bury it or pretend it away, but to bring it to Him honestly. Grief is not a single moment but a passage, and it moves through recognizable seasons: the first numb shock and disbelief; then anger, and we may be honest with God about anger; then the bargaining and guilt, the endless "if only I had"; then the depression when reality finally settles its full weight; and at last, by grace, acceptance. There is no shortcut through these waters and no shame in passing through them. The Lord Jesus Himself wept at the tomb of Lazarus, though He knew He would raise him minutes later. To mourn is not a failure of faith. It is the honest heart carrying its sorrow to the only One who can truly comfort it, rather than to the lesser comforts that cannot hold its weight.
blocks.es_reference: La segunda respuesta es dar a Dios nuestro dolor — no enterrarlo ni fingir que no existe, sino traerlo a Él honestamente. El dolor no es un solo momento sino un paso, y se mueve por etapas reconocibles: la primera conmoción entumecida y la incredulidad; luego la ira, y podemos ser honestos con Dios acerca de la ira; luego el regateo y la culpa, el interminable "si tan solo hubiera"; luego la depresión cuando la realidad al fin asienta todo su peso; y por último, por gracia, la aceptación. No hay atajo a través de estas aguas ni vergüenza en atravesarlas. El mismo Señor Jesús lloró ante la tumba de Lázaro, aunque sabía que lo resucitaría minutos después. Llorar no es un fracaso de la fe. Es el corazón honesto llevando su tristeza al único que puede consolarlo de veras, en lugar de a los consuelos menores que no pueden sostener su peso.

blocks.en: And we should learn from this how to comfort others, because much of pastoral ministry is simply being present in another's grief. Often the help a sufferer needs is not an explanation. Joe Bayly, who buried three of his own children, wrote of two visitors in his sorrow. One spoke constantly — of God's purposes, of hope beyond the grave; everything he said was true, and Bayly was unmoved and only wished he would leave. The other simply sat beside him, said little, listened, prayed briefly, and went. "I was comforted," Bayly wrote. "I hated to see him go." The grieving need our presence more than our paragraphs.
blocks.es_reference: Y debemos aprender de esto cómo consolar a otros, porque gran parte del ministerio pastoral es sencillamente estar presente en el dolor ajeno. A menudo la ayuda que necesita el que sufre no es una explicación. Joe Bayly, que sepultó a tres de sus propios hijos, escribió de dos visitantes en su dolor. Uno habló sin cesar — de los propósitos de Dios, de la esperanza más allá de la tumba; todo lo que decía era cierto, y Bayly quedó indiferente y solo deseaba que se fuera. El otro simplemente se sentó a su lado, dijo poco, escuchó, oró brevemente, y se fue. "Fui consolado," escribió Bayly. "Lamenté verlo irse." Los que sufren necesitan nuestra presencia más que nuestros párrafos.

blocks.en: 7. Give God Your Burden
blocks.es_reference: 7. Dé a Dios Su Carga

blocks.en: The third response is the heart of the psalm: actually to hand God the burden, rolling it off our shoulders and onto His. Some griefs are so great they threaten to knock the props out from under us entirely, until we feel that life itself should simply stop. It is exactly there, at the breaking point, that the promise of verse 22 is meant to bear our weight: "He shall sustain you; He shall never permit the righteous to be moved."
blocks.es_reference: La tercera respuesta es el corazón del salmo: entregar realmente a Dios la carga, quitándola de nuestros hombros y poniéndola sobre los Suyos. Algunos dolores son tan grandes que amenazan con derribar por completo los puntales de debajo de nosotros, hasta que sentimos que la vida misma debería sencillamente detenerse. Es exactamente allí, en el punto de quiebre, donde la promesa del versículo 22 está destinada a llevar nuestro peso: "Él te sustentará; no dejará para siempre caído al justo."

blocks.en: What does it look like when a believer truly gives God the burden? It looks like a person living above their circumstances while the grief is still real. Consider the missionary Eric Barker, who sent his wife and eight children to safety by ship during the Second World War. The Sunday after they sailed he told his congregation, "I have just received word that all my family have arrived safely home," and went on with the service — for he had been handed a telegram minutes earlier saying the ship was torpedoed and all aboard had drowned. He could stand because he knew his family were believers safely with God, and that knowledge held him up above a grief that would otherwise have crushed him. To cast the burden is not to feel nothing; it is to stand on something deeper than the loss.
blocks.es_reference: ¿Cómo se ve cuando un creyente de veras le da a Dios la carga? Se ve como una persona que vive por encima de sus circunstancias mientras el dolor sigue siendo real. Considere al misionero Eric Barker, que envió a su esposa y sus ocho hijos a un lugar seguro en barco durante la Segunda Guerra Mundial. El domingo después de que zarparon, dijo a su congregación: "Acabo de recibir noticia de que toda mi familia ha llegado a salvo a casa," y siguió con el culto — porque minutos antes le habían entregado un telegrama diciendo que el barco había sido torpedeado y que todos a bordo se habían ahogado. Pudo mantenerse de pie porque sabía que su familia eran creyentes, a salvo con Dios, y ese conocimiento lo sostuvo por encima de un dolor que de otro modo lo habría aplastado. Echar la carga no es no sentir nada; es estar de pie sobre algo más profundo que la pérdida.

blocks.en: 8. A Why That Bears Any How
blocks.es_reference: 8. Un "Porqué" que Soporta Cualquier "Cómo"

blocks.en: Underneath all three responses lies one foundation: the believer has been given a reason to endure that the world can neither supply nor remove. When the burden is heaviest, what sustains us is not a technique but a Person, and the meaning He gives to our lives even in the dark.
blocks.es_reference: Debajo de las tres respuestas hay un solo fundamento: al creyente se le ha dado una razón para perseverar que el mundo no puede suministrar ni quitar. Cuando la carga es más pesada, lo que nos sostiene no es una técnica sino una Persona, y el sentido que Él da a nuestra vida aun en la oscuridad.

blocks.en: "He Who Has a Why": The psychiatrist Viktor Frankl was stripped of everything at Auschwitz — his family, his property, even the manuscript of his life's work hidden in his coat. He wondered whether his life held any meaning at all. Then, forced to trade his clothes, he found in the pocket of a dead man's coat a single page torn from a Hebrew prayer book: the Shema, "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one… you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart." He took it as a summons to live his beliefs rather than merely write them, and later concluded, "He who has a 'why' to live for can bear almost any 'how.'"
blocks.es_reference: "El que Tiene un Porqué": El psiquiatra Viktor Frankl fue despojado de todo en Auschwitz — su familia, sus bienes, hasta el manuscrito de la obra de su vida escondido en su abrigo. Se preguntó si su vida tenía algún sentido. Entonces, obligado a cambiar de ropa, halló en el bolsillo del abrigo de un hombre muerto una sola página arrancada de un libro de oración hebreo: el Shemá, "Oye, Israel: Jehová nuestro Dios, Jehová uno es… amarás a Jehová tu Dios de todo tu corazón." Lo tomó como un llamado a vivir sus creencias en lugar de solo escribirlas, y luego concluyó: "El que tiene un 'porqué' para vivir puede soportar casi cualquier 'cómo.'"

blocks.en: That is the final word of Psalm 55. The believer has a "why" the world cannot give and cannot take away — a God who sustains, a heaven that waits, and a love from which, as Paul wrote, not even death can separate us. So when life tumbles in, do not carry the burden alone, and do not turn for relief to comforts too small to hold you. Give God your thanks, give Him your grief, and give Him the burden itself. Cast it on the LORD, and He will sustain you; like Hopeful stepping into the cold river, you will find the bottom is sound.
blocks.es_reference: Esa es la palabra final del Salmo 55. El creyente tiene un "porqué" que el mundo no puede dar ni quitar — un Dios que sustenta, un cielo que espera, y un amor del cual, como escribió Pablo, ni la muerte puede separarnos. Así que cuando la vida se derrumbe, no lleve la carga a solas, ni se vuelva por alivio a consuelos demasiado pequeños para sostenerle. Dé a Dios su gratitud, déle su dolor, y déle la carga misma. Échela sobre Jehová, y Él le sustentará; como Esperanzado entrando en el río frío, hallará que el fondo es firme.

mc.stem: What is the single steadying command at the center of Psalm 55, on which this lesson is built?
options: "The LORD is my shepherd"
"Be still, and know that I am God"
"Cast your burden on the LORD, and He shall sustain you"
"Create in me a clean heart"
mc.why: The whole lesson rests on one command: 'Cast your burden on the LORD, and He shall sustain you.'

mc.stem: How does David describe his own condition in Psalm 55, before he arrives at the command to cast his burden?
options: Calm and untroubled
Overwhelmed, his heart severely pained, longing for wings to fly away
Proud and self-sufficient
Indifferent to his trouble
mc.why: David begins overwhelmed, his heart severely pained, longing for wings to fly away — he does not pretend the burden is light.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, what does the word translated "cast" actually picture?
options: A gentle, gradual setting-down
Quietly worrying in a more religious way
Ignoring the burden until it passes
A deliberate throwing of a heavy load off oneself onto another
mc.why: 'Cast' means a deliberate throwing of a heavy load off ourselves onto Another — an act of the will, not mere worry.

mc.stem: Which New Testament verse echoes Psalm 55:22 about casting our care on God?
options: 1 Peter 5:7 — "casting all your care upon Him, for He cares for you"
Romans 8:28
Philippians 4:13
John 3:16
mc.why: Peter echoes this verse in 1 Peter 5:7: 'casting all your care upon Him, for He cares for you.'

mc.stem: What exactly does God promise in return when we cast our burden, according to the lesson?
options: To remove every burden immediately
To sustain us — to hold us up so we are not toppled, not necessarily to remove the burden
To explain why the trial came
To reward us with wealth
mc.why: God promises to sustain us — to hold us up so we are not toppled — not necessarily to remove the burden itself.

mc.stem: The lesson likens the sustained believer to what image?
options: A ship without an anchor
A candle in the wind
A tree in a storm whose roots hold — it bends but never falls
A house built on sand
mc.why: The sustained believer is like a tree in a storm whose roots hold: it bends under the wind but never falls.

mc.stem: Who was Arthur John Gossip, and what was the sermon he preached just after his wife's sudden death?
options: A Scottish preacher; "But When Life Tumbles In, What Then?"
An English bishop; "The Problem of Pain"
An American evangelist; "Amazing Grace"
A missionary; "The Cost of Discipleship"
mc.why: Arthur John Gossip, a Scottish preacher, preached 'But When Life Tumbles In, What Then?' just after his wife's sudden death.

mc.stem: What question did Gossip ask those tempted to turn away from God in grief?
options: "Why does God allow suffering?"
"How long, O Lord?"
"What have we done to deserve this?"
"Where else is there to turn?"
mc.why: To those tempted to abandon God in grief, Gossip asked the question with no other answer: 'Where else is there to turn?'

mc.stem: In Gethsemane, what does the lesson highlight about how the Father answered Jesus' prayer?
options: He remained silent and absent
He removed the cup at once
He did not remove the cup, but did not desert Him — He gave strength and peace to finish
He sent the disciples to help
mc.why: In Gethsemane the Father did not remove the cup, but did not desert His Son — He gave strength and peace to finish.

mc.stem: How does Gethsemane reshape what we should expect when we cast a burden on God?
options: The burden always vanishes instantly
God only helps with small troubles
We should not pray about burdens at all
Often He leaves the weight on us but puts His strength underneath it
mc.why: Gethsemane reshapes our expectation: often God leaves the weight on us but puts His own strength underneath it.

mc.stem: The first of the three responses to a burden is to give God your thanks. What does 1 Thessalonians 5:18 actually say?
options: Give thanks only when things go well
Give thanks IN everything (not necessarily FOR everything)
Give thanks once a day
Give thanks only in public worship
mc.why: 1 Thessalonians 5:18 says give thanks IN everything, not necessarily FOR everything — gratitude even within the trial.

mc.stem: According to the lesson, how do self-pity and bitterness work, and how does thanksgiving counter them?
options: They narrow vision until the burden hides God; thanksgiving pries that vision back open
They have no effect either way
They help us grieve; thanksgiving prevents grief
They strengthen faith; thanksgiving weakens it
mc.why: Self-pity and bitterness narrow our vision until the burden hides God; thanksgiving pries that vision back open.

mc.stem: How does the missionary Eric Barker illustrate "living above" one's circumstances?

mc.stem: Finding a page of the Shema in Auschwitz became, for Viktor Frankl, a summons to do what?

Only the strong survive

Suffering has no meaning
mc.why: Frankl concluded, and the lesson applies to Psalm 55: 'He who has a why to live for can bear almost any how.'

sa.prompt: Describe the situation from which Psalm 55 is written, and the single command at its center.
sa.model: Psalm 55 is written from a place of crushing distress. David describes himself as overwhelmed, his heart severely pained within him, even longing for wings like a dove so he could fly away and be at rest. Part of his anguish is betrayal by a close friend. Out of that very real trouble comes the single steadying command at the center of the psalm: "Cast your burden on the LORD, and He shall sustain you." The psalm is honest that the burden is heavy and the pain real; it does not pretend otherwise, but it points the troubled heart to the one place the load can be laid down.

sa.prompt: Explain what the word "cast" means in Psalm 55:22 and what God promises in return.
sa.model: The word "cast" in Psalm 55:22 pictures a deliberate, decisive act, throwing a heavy load off oneself and onto another, the way you would heave a weight off your shoulders. It is not vague worrying but an act of the will, handing the burden over to God. In return God promises to sustain us: "He shall sustain you; He shall never permit the righteous to be moved." The promise is not necessarily that He will lift the trouble away, but that He will hold us up under it so we are not toppled. We do the casting; God does the sustaining.

sa.prompt: The lesson says God promises to sustain rather than always remove the burden. Explain the difference and the tree image.
sa.model: The lesson draws a careful distinction: God promises to sustain us, not always to remove the burden. We often want Him to take the trouble away, but His promise is to hold us up while we carry it, supplying strength underneath the weight. The tree image captures it: a tree in a storm is not spared the wind, but its roots hold, so that it bends without being uprooted. So the sustained believer may still feel the full force of the trial, yet is kept from falling because God is holding him. The burden may remain, but we are upheld in the midst of it.

sa.prompt: What does Arthur John Gossip's response after his wife's sudden death teach about faith when life tumbles in?
sa.model: Arthur John Gossip was a Scottish preacher whose wife died suddenly. Soon after, he preached a sermon titled "But When Life Tumbles In, What Then?" Out of his own raw grief he did not abandon his faith but pressed into it, asking those tempted to turn away from God in sorrow the question that has no other answer: "Where else is there to turn?" His response teaches that when life collapses, faith is not the denial of grief but the decision to keep holding to God because there is nowhere better to go. In the darkest hour, the believer casts himself on the only One who can sustain.

sa.prompt: Explain how Gethsemane shows the way God answers when we cast a burden on Him.
sa.model: Gethsemane shows how God often answers when we cast a burden on Him. Jesus prayed that the cup might pass, yet the Father did not remove it; instead He did not desert His Son but strengthened Him to drink it and finish His work. So when we cast our burden on God, He frequently does not take the weight away but puts His own strength underneath us so we can bear it. This reshapes our expectation: the answer to "cast your burden" is not always relief from the trouble, but the sustaining grace and presence of God that carry us through it, as they carried Jesus through the cross.

sa.prompt: Explain the first response, giving God your thanks, including what 1 Thessalonians 5:18 does and does not say.
sa.model: The first response to a burden is to give God your thanks. The lesson is precise about what 1 Thessalonians 5:18 actually says: give thanks IN everything, not necessarily FOR everything. We are not told to be glad about the trouble itself, but to find reasons for gratitude even within it, remembering God's goodness in the midst of pain. This matters because self-pity and bitterness narrow our vision until the burden blots out God; thanksgiving pries that vision back open, helping us see that God is still present and still good even when the load is heavy. Gratitude reorders how we see the trial.

sa.prompt: Explain the second response, giving God your grief, including the seasons grief moves through.
sa.model: The second response is to give God your grief, bringing our sorrow honestly to Him rather than hiding it. The lesson reminds us that Jesus Himself wept at the tomb of Lazarus, so to mourn is not a failure of faith but a part of being human before God. Grief moves through seasons; it is not a single moment but a process of shock, sorrow, and slow healing, and God walks with us through all of it. We are not asked to pretend we feel nothing or to rush past the pain. Casting our grief on God means weeping in His presence, trusting that He receives our tears.

sa.prompt: Using Joe Bayly's two visitors, explain how we should comfort those who grieve.
sa.model: Joe Bayly, who had lost children, recalled two visitors in his grief. One talked at length, offered explanations and arguments, and left him cold; the other simply sat with him, listened, said little, and prayed briefly, and that one brought comfort. The lesson draws a clear principle for comforting the grieving: they need our presence more than our paragraphs. Words, especially explanations and tidy answers, often wound rather than help; what heals is a quiet, loving presence that is willing to sit in the sorrow with the sufferer. To comfort well is to come close and stay near, not to fix it with speech.

sa.prompt: Explain the third response, giving God the burden, and how Eric Barker illustrates living above one's circumstances.
sa.model: The third response is to give God the burden itself, the deliberate casting of Psalm 55:22, trusting His promise: "He shall sustain you; He shall never permit the righteous to be moved." Eric Barker illustrates living above one's circumstances: a missionary who learned that his family had drowned at sea, yet stood up and led his congregation in worship that very hour, because he knew they were safely home with God. He did not feel nothing; he stood on something deeper than his loss. Casting the burden is not the absence of pain but the choice to rest the whole weight on God and remain standing in Him.

sa.prompt: Explain the foundation under all three responses, using Frankl's conclusion about a why and a how.
sa.model: Under all three responses lies one foundation: a reason to trust God that is deeper than the trouble. Viktor Frankl, who survived the death camps, concluded that "he who has a why to live for can bear almost any how." The lesson applies this to Psalm 55: when we know the why, that God is good, present, and working out His purpose, we can bear almost any how, any burden or sorrow. The foundation is not our circumstances or our feelings but the trustworthy character of God. Because He sustains the one who casts his burden on Him, we have a why strong enough to carry us through any how.
